units: two woodworking shops stand on the same street
the first shop shapes wood by hand with plain tools
the second shop uses machines and employs three workers
the workers in the second shop mostly watch screens
the hand shop turns out little but sells at a steep price
the mechanized shop turns out a lot and sells cheaply
the hand shop depends on its reputation to survive
the mechanized shop depends on the flow of orders
the two owners greet each other in the evening
text: Two woodworking shops stand on the same street, barely a doorway apart. In the first, a seasoned joiner shapes every board by hand at a workbench holding nothing beyond plain, unremarkable tools. In the second, machinery slices identical planks throughout the day, and the three workers there watch screens considerably more than they handle timber. The handmade shop produces very little, yet each piece departs at a steep price, since the buyer purchases patience alongside the wood. The mechanized shop dispatches crate after crate cheaply, counting on volume to cover heavier overheads. One survives as long as people keep praising the work of the hand. The other survives as long as orders keep arriving. At closing time the two owners nod across the street, aware that they sell the same object by opposite routes.

units: the writer names three weaknesses in stock management
the first weakness concerns forecasting demand
forecasts rest on old records with no correction
warehouses fill up with goods nobody buys
the second weakness concerns the costing of goods
a surplus of goods ties up cash needed elsewhere
the third weakness concerns how buyers behave
managers order too much for fear of running short
the writer holds that fixing the forecast alone will not do
text: Three weaknesses eat away at the way midsized manufacturers handle their stock, and they deserve plain names. The first is forecasting. Demand gets projected from old records, with no correction for the supply breaks that distorted them, so warehouses fill up with goods nobody buys. The second is costing. A surplus batch ties up cash that will be missing elsewhere, and a crowded storeroom soon costs real money to keep. The third is behavior. Managers order heavy rather than face an empty shelf, an instinct anyone can understand and one that quietly drains the accounts. A losing year rarely comes from a single mistake. It comes from three habits that feed one another. Fixing the forecast while leaving untouched whatever rewards the buyers will bring nothing but brief relief.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the person described runs a weaving cooperative
she started out as an apprentice at a hand loom
her first job was mending broken threads
the experienced weavers gladly handed that job to her
she was then moved to the receiving of raw materials
that post taught her about prices and delays
she trained in bookkeeping away from the workshop
she proposed selling without going through a middleman
takings climbed and the workshop hired more staff
text: The woman who runs a weaving cooperative began there as an apprentice at a hand loom. Her first job was tying broken threads back together, painstaking work that the more experienced weavers were glad to hand off to her. After two seasons she was moved to the receiving dock, where the raw materials came in, and that post taught her about prices, delays, and margins. She left the workshop for a spell of training in bookkeeping, then came back with one clear proposal: sell straight to the shops instead of going through a middleman who took his cut. The cooperative hesitated, then agreed to a small trial. Takings climbed, and the workshop hired two more spinners. She now heads the place she knew as a child, and she gives the delicate orders to the apprentices, the way it was once done for her.

units: a training scheme for jobseekers is under review
the scheme is judged useful but poorly calibrated
the modules teach motions that are too narrow
employers want people able to move from one station to another
trainees find work but leave it quickly
the reviewer blames the departures on the narrowness of the training
the stretches spent inside a company give better results
the reviewer calls for those company stretches to be lengthened
text: The training scheme under review delivers a genuine service, but its calibration invites serious argument. Its modules teach narrow motions, tailored to a single task, while employers are asking for people who can move from one station to another as the order book shifts. The mismatch produces an effect you can measure: trainees land a job quickly enough, then walk away before the probationary period ends, unable to cope with the secondary duties dropped on them. The stretches spent inside a company turn out far better, probably because the trainee watches the whole chain there rather than one isolated link. The review therefore calls for those stretches to be lengthened, even at the cost of the classroom hours, which look redundant beside the manuals handed out on the very first day.

units: the writer writes to a friend about his soap business
making the soap by hand swallows all his evenings
the profits stayed too thin at the start
the shipping costs ate up the margin
the writer cut his catalogue down to three scents
he now delivers to a shared depot instead of sending each parcel
the business has turned profitable since these changes
the writer invites his friend to come and see the workshop
text: I owe you news about the soap business, and this letter arrives considerably late. You remember what I used to complain about: making everything by hand swallowed all my evenings, and the profits remained stubbornly thin. I finally identified the culprit, and it was shipping. Every parcel went out on its own, with its own box and its own paperwork, and the margin melted away before the order ever reached the buyer. So I cut. I brought the catalogue down to three scents, the ones that always moved, and I stopped chasing single orders. My crates now go to a shared depot, and the retailers come and take what they need. Since then the business is genuinely profitable, and I sleep. Come and see the workshop when you pass through. You will judge the difference, and you will go home loaded up.

units: an economist answers questions about how young firms raise money
she compares a bank loan with bringing an investor into the capital
a loan must be repaid even when trade falls off
a loan leaves the founder in command of his own decisions
an investor asks for nothing if the venture fails
an investor demands a share of the decisions and of later profits
she advises a loan for businesses with steady takings
she advises opening the capital for uncertain and costly ventures
text: An economist specializing in the financing of young firms agrees to take questions. Borrow, or bring in a partner? She refuses to settle it in a word and sets the two side by side. A loan, she explains, imposes a due date that arrives whether or not sales hold up, yet it leaves the founder in full command of every decision. Bringing an investor into the capital demands nothing should the venture fail, but it sells off a share of the decisions and of whatever profit comes later. So which does she advise? A business with dependable takings carries a fixed due date easily and does well to borrow. An uncertain venture, expensive to launch and slow to repay, rarely holds up without a partner willing to wait. The real question, she says, is how regular the incoming receipts will be.

units: two market women talk after the covered market closes
the fruit seller lists her troubles
she mentions the rent on her stall
she mentions the crates of damaged goods
she mentions the supplier who arrives late
the cheese seller answers that her own troubles differ
the cheese seller mentions the cold she has to hold steady
the cheese seller mentions the falling number of customers
the two women agree to share a van
text: The shutters of the covered market had just come down when the fruit seller began her inventory of troubles. She talked about the rent on her stall, which climbed every season while the aisle remained as shabby as ever. She talked about the battered crates, the bruised peaches that no customer would ever take and that she would carry home at night. She talked about her supplier, whose van pulled in after opening, once the shoppers had already come and gone. The cheese seller heard her out, then said her own troubles answered to entirely different names: the cold, hard to hold steady, the power bill that followed from it, and the line of customers thinning week after week. The two of them fell silent for a moment. Then they agreed to rent a van together and go for their crates before dawn.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text traces the rise of the trade associations
the first craftsmen were scattered and had no common rules
neighboring shops first agreed on matching measurements
the next agreement covered the length of apprenticeship
the associations then set floor prices
the floor prices sheltered members from competing on rates
the associations also decided who could open a shop
that closing of the door ended up holding back untried methods
the associations lost their power as the manufactories grew
text: Before any organization existed, the craftsmen of a single trade worked in isolation, each on his own, with no shared measure and no rule in common. The first agreement between neighboring shops covered size: a board, a pot, a length of cloth had to match one gauge, or else a buyer had no way to compare. Apprenticeship came next, and its length and its stages were duly established. The trade associations, thriving by then, extended their grip further and fixed a floor beneath prices, which sheltered their members from ruinous undercutting. In the end they took for themselves the right to say who could open a shop, and that closing of the door, protective at the start, discouraged untried methods. Once the manufactories gathered hundreds of workers under one roof, these associations lost their hold.

units: the text explains why a farm product rises in price after a poor harvest
a thin harvest shrinks the quantity on offer
the buyers turn up in the same numbers as before
the scarcity drives up the price paid to the grower
the processors pass that rise on to their own charges
some buyers turn to a replacement product
the added demand drives up the price of the replacement too
prices come back down when the next harvest is plentiful
text: A meager harvest does more than merely empty the barns. It sets off a chain of effects that reaches all the way to the market stall. The available quantity dwindles while just as many buyers turn up as before, so each of them agrees to pay more to get a share, and the price paid to the grower climbs. The firms that transform the crop watch their own invoices swell, and they pass the weight on to what they charge. Part of the trade gives up at that point and switches to a neighboring product. That migration carries a consequence that few people anticipate: the replacement, suddenly in heavy demand, grows dearer in its turn, even though its own harvest was perfectly ordinary. Equilibrium returns only with a generous season, when the barns fill again and the pressure on prices eases.

units: a village bakery threw away part of its output every evening
the baker baked the same quantity without regard to sales
the waste threatened the finances of the shop
the apprentice wrote down the unsold loaves for several weeks
the record showed that the losses piled up at the end of the week
the end-of-week batch was cut back
the leftover loaves are sold cheaply before closing
the waste fell sharply
a neighboring shop copied the method
text: Every evening the baker in a valley village filled a sack with the loaves nobody had bought, and the sack went off to a farm nearby. He had baked the same quantity since the day he opened, without once looking at what sold, and the waste was devouring a margin already thin. The apprentice suggested counting. For several weeks she wrote down in a notebook how many loaves went unsold, their shape, the flour used. The record was merciless: the losses piled up at the end of the week, when families baked at home. So the last batch of the week was cut by a third, and whatever sat on the shelf half an hour before closing was sold off at a knockdown price. The waste shrank, the till breathed, and the shopkeeper across the way, who had been watching, began keeping an identical notebook.
